courseDetails.title: Writing for the Media
courseDetails.description: A 100-level Mass Communication course covering media-writing responsibilities, grammar and syntax, platform-specific styles, research and reference materials, print and script structures, news and feature writing, opinion ethics, and multimedia storytelling.

questions.question: What is the mass media writer's most fundamental responsibility before publishing a story?
options: Publishing before competitors without checking facts
Promoting the writer's personal interests
Gathering and verifying accurate information
Making the story as long as possible
questions.explanation: A media writer must confirm information through research, interviews, and fact-checking because accuracy builds public trust and prevents misinformation.

questions.question: Why should a media writer adapt the tone and length of a story for different platforms?
options: Longer content is always more credible
All platforms legally require identical wording
Adaptation removes the need for research
Each platform has different audience habits and communication requirements
questions.explanation: Radio, television, print, and digital media are consumed differently, so writers adjust language, tone, structure, and length to suit each medium.

questions.question: A reporter receives a dramatic claim from an anonymous social media account. What should the reporter do first?
options: Verify the claim through credible and independent sources
Remove the source's name and treat it as confirmed
Rewrite it as personal opinion
Publish it immediately and correct it later
questions.explanation: Speed does not replace verification. The claim should be checked against reliable evidence and independent sources before publication.

questions.question: Which action best demonstrates that a media writer understands audience needs?
options: Choosing language and examples appropriate to the target readers
Using the same technical vocabulary for every audience
Ignoring feedback from readers
Writing only about topics the writer personally enjoys
questions.explanation: Audience awareness helps a writer select suitable language, examples, detail, and tone so the message is relevant and understandable.

questions.question: Which practice is inconsistent with ethical media writing?
options: Presenting an unverified rumour as a confirmed fact
Respecting legitimate privacy concerns
Correcting a factual error promptly
Avoiding plagiarism
questions.explanation: Ethical writing requires accuracy, verification, respect for privacy, and honesty. Presenting rumours as facts misleads the audience.

questions.question: Why is engaging content important in a crowded media environment?
options: It guarantees that every reader agrees with the writer
It helps capture and retain the audience's attention
It removes the need for a clear structure
It allows facts to be replaced with entertainment
questions.explanation: Clear, relatable, and compelling storytelling helps a message stand out while still preserving accuracy and ethical standards.

questions.question: Which combination best describes the work of a responsible mass media writer?
options: Writing only for print and ignoring audience feedback
Copying popular stories, exaggerating claims, and avoiding corrections
Focusing on speed, opinion, and commercial gain alone
Researching, writing clearly, adapting to platforms, and observing ethics
questions.explanation: The role combines information gathering, verification, audience awareness, platform adaptation, clear writing, and ethical judgement.

questions.question: A television script merely repeats every detail already visible on screen. What is the main weakness?
options: The words fail to complement the visuals
The programme contains too many verified facts
The writer has used the inverted pyramid
The script is too objective
questions.explanation: Television writing should add context, explanation, or meaning to the pictures rather than simply describing what viewers can already see.

questions.question: Which sentence shows correct subject-verb agreement?
options: The journalists writing their reports every morning.
The journalists write their reports every morning.
The journalist write their report every morning.
The journalists writes their reports every morning.
questions.explanation: The plural subject 'journalists' correctly takes the plural verb 'write'.

questions.question: Which revision maintains consistent past tense?
options: The reporter had interview the witness and submits the story.
The reporter interviewed the witness and submitted the story.
The reporter interviews the witness and submitted the story.
The reporter interviewed the witness and submits the story.
questions.explanation: Both actions occurred in the past, so 'interviewed' and 'submitted' maintain a clear timeline.

questions.question: What is the main function of syntax in media writing?
options: Selecting the station's broadcast frequency
Determining the legal ownership of a newspaper
Measuring the size of an audience
Arranging words and phrases so sentences are logical and clear
questions.explanation: Syntax concerns word and phrase arrangement. Proper syntax makes the intended meaning easier to understand.

questions.question: Which sentence contains a dangling modifier?
options: Hoping to publish quickly, the article was written before noon.
Before noon, the journalist carefully completed the article.
The journalist finished the article before noon because the deadline was near.
Hoping to publish quickly, the journalist finished the article before noon.
questions.explanation: The opening phrase logically describes the journalist, not the article. The sentence wrongly makes the article appear to be doing the hoping.

questions.question: Which option is a sentence fragment?
options: The journalist reported from the flooded community.
The journalist interviewed residents and recorded their experiences.
While reporting from the flooded community, the journalist interviewed residents.
While reporting from the flooded community.
questions.explanation: The phrase begins with a dependent clause but does not contain an independent clause that completes the thought.

questions.question: Which sentence is written in the clearest active voice?
options: The headline was approved by the editor.
The editor approved the headline.
Approval of the headline was made by the editor.
The headline had been approved by the editor.
questions.explanation: In active voice, the subject performs the action directly: the editor approved the headline.

questions.question: When is passive voice most justifiable in media writing?
options: When the person performing the action is unknown or unimportant
When a sentence should be made as long as possible
Whenever the writer wants to hide every source
Whenever the subject is a journalist
questions.explanation: Active voice is generally clearer, but passive voice can be useful when the doer is unknown, irrelevant, or less important than the action.

questions.question: Which punctuation mark is most suitable for introducing a list after a complete clause?
options: A colon
A question mark
An apostrophe
A hyphen
questions.explanation: A colon introduces a list, explanation, or elaboration after a complete clause.

questions.question: Which punctuation mark can correctly link two closely related independent clauses?
options: A semicolon
A full stop followed by no new sentence
A quotation mark
An apostrophe
questions.explanation: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses without using a coordinating conjunction.

questions.question: Which sentence is a compound sentence?
options: The protest ended peacefully.
The protest ended peacefully, and the police left the scene.
Ending peacefully after several hours.
Although the protest ended peacefully, the police remained nearby.
questions.explanation: A compound sentence contains two independent clauses joined here by the coordinating conjunction 'and'.

questions.question: Which sentence is complex?
options: The peaceful protest ended.
The protest was peaceful, and the crowd dispersed.
Although the protest was peaceful, the police remained on standby.
The protest was peaceful.
questions.explanation: A complex sentence has one dependent clause and at least one independent clause.

questions.question: Why does broadcast writing usually use conversational and simple language?
options: Simple language is required only for advertisements
The audience normally hears the message rather than reading it repeatedly
Listeners can always pause a live bulletin
Broadcast scripts must contain more jargon than print
questions.explanation: Listeners often have one opportunity to understand a broadcast, so natural, direct language improves comprehension.

questions.question: What is a major advantage of the inverted pyramid in newspaper writing?
options: It requires the conclusion to contain all essential facts
It is designed mainly for personal essays
Readers receive the most important information first
It prevents editors from shortening articles
questions.explanation: The structure begins with the key facts, allowing readers to understand the story quickly and editors to trim from the bottom.

questions.question: Which feature is especially associated with digital media writing?
options: Short paragraphs, subheadings, hyperlinks, and relevant keywords
No concern for searchability
Only long uninterrupted paragraphs
Complete avoidance of images and video
questions.explanation: Digital writing is designed for screen reading and discovery, so it uses scannable structure, links, multimedia, and SEO.

questions.question: How have character limits on social media influenced media writing?
options: They require every post to use academic language
They make fact-checking unnecessary
They encourage concise and attention-grabbing messages
They eliminate the need for visual content
questions.explanation: Limited space pushes writers to communicate quickly and directly while using hooks, hashtags, and visuals strategically.

questions.question: What does convergence journalism require from a modern media writer?
options: The ability to think and work across several media formats
Writing the same version of a story for every platform
Avoidance of images, audio, and video
Exclusive concentration on printed newspapers
questions.explanation: Convergence combines text, audio, images, video, and interactive elements, so writers need adaptable multimedia skills.

questions.question: A web article is divided into short paragraphs with descriptive subheadings. What audience behaviour is the writer addressing?
options: Readers prefer all information hidden in footnotes
Readers cannot understand headlines
Readers often scan screens instead of reading every word in sequence
Online audiences reject concise writing
questions.explanation: Scannable formatting lets users locate key information quickly on screens.

questions.question: What should a television writer do when strong visuals already show the main action?
options: Describe every visible movement word for word
Replace the visuals with a long written paragraph
Use the script to add context or information the pictures do not provide
Remove all narration regardless of the story
questions.explanation: Effective television writing complements rather than duplicates the images.

questions.question: A science reporter understands a medical study but is writing for the general public. What is the best approach?
options: Copy the study's technical wording without explanation
Replace the evidence with personal experience
Omit important limitations to make the story exciting
Explain the findings accurately in clear, non-technical language
questions.explanation: Science and health writers must understand specialised material and translate it accurately without unnecessary jargon.

questions.question: Why should a business reporter understand financial statements and market trends?
options: To convert every business story into political commentary
To avoid discussing the significance of company results
To explain what financial figures mean and how they affect the wider economy
To report figures without checking their context
questions.explanation: Economic knowledge helps the reporter interpret numbers rather than merely repeat them.

questions.question: Which background knowledge is most useful when covering an election?
options: Only computer programming languages
Only film criticism and fashion trends
Political systems, history, parties, voting patterns, and social issues
Only advertising design
questions.explanation: Political journalism requires context so the reporter can explain the importance of parties, issues, policies, and voting behaviour.

questions.question: A journalist covering a new artificial intelligence system should explain both how it works and what else?
options: The writer's unrelated political preferences
Its possible social effects, such as privacy concerns and job automation
Why all technology is automatically beneficial
Only the colour of the company's logo
questions.explanation: Technology reporting should connect technical details with wider ethical, economic, and social implications.

questions.question: What enables an arts reporter to produce more than a surface-level review of an exhibition?
options: Describing only the size of the venue
Avoiding any background research
Using financial statistics as the sole basis of the review
Knowledge of art history, cultural context, and social trends
questions.explanation: Cultural knowledge allows the writer to interpret meaning, style, historical influence, and social significance.

questions.question: Why does environmental journalism often require cross-disciplinary knowledge?
options: Environmental stories contain no factual claims
Environmental issues involve science, public policy, and economic consequences
Only photographs are needed to explain climate issues
Environmental reporting is identical to celebrity reporting
questions.explanation: A complete environmental story may need scientific explanation, policy analysis, and discussion of costs or economic effects.

questions.question: Which reference material is most suitable as a starting point for general background on an unfamiliar topic?
options: A random anonymous message
An encyclopaedia
An unverified comment section
A personal advertisement
questions.explanation: Encyclopaedias provide broad introductory information, though recent developments should be checked elsewhere.

questions.question: What is the main journalistic use of a specialised dictionary?
options: Verifying the meaning and correct use of technical terms
Supplying current election results
Providing eyewitness testimony
Replacing all subject experts
questions.explanation: Legal, medical, and other specialised dictionaries help writers understand and use field-specific language accurately.

questions.question: Why is an interview classified as a primary source?
options: It provides first-hand information from an expert, witness, or participant
It contains only the journalist's interpretation
It is always published in a textbook
It summarises several old newspaper articles
questions.explanation: An interview gives direct testimony, perspectives, and quotations from someone with relevant knowledge or experience.

questions.question: Which source is generally best for detailed peer-reviewed findings on a scientific subject?
options: An entertainment advert
An anonymous social media meme
A fictional short story
A scholarly journal
questions.explanation: Scholarly journals publish expert research that has usually undergone peer review, making them valuable for specialised reporting.

questions.question: A journalist wants to compare today's flood with similar floods reported ten years ago. Which source is most useful?
options: A spelling dictionary
A trusted news archive
A product brochure
A blank notebook
questions.explanation: News archives provide historical reports that help journalists compare events and add context.

questions.question: Which reference source is most appropriate for current population, health, or economic figures?
options: A personal diary
A reliable statistical database
A feature film
An unsourced opinion column
questions.explanation: Government and recognised research databases provide concrete, current data for stories involving numbers.

questions.question: How should a journalist use a quick online reference such as Wikipedia?
options: Treat every statement as final and unquestionable
Quote it without checking its cited sources
Use it instead of official documents in all cases
Use it for orientation, then cross-check important claims with authoritative sources
questions.explanation: Open online tools can help identify leads, but journalists should verify facts through official records, recognised databases, or other credible sources.

questions.question: What was a major limitation of the typewriter compared with a word processor?
options: It could not produce readable text
It required internet access
It automatically changed the writer's meaning
Correcting mistakes could require retyping entire sections
questions.explanation: Typewriters produced legible copy but offered little editing flexibility, so substantial corrections often meant retyping.

questions.question: Why do many field reporters still carry a notebook and pen?
options: They automatically verify every fact
They record high-quality video
They remain portable and usable when power or internet access fails
They can publish directly to a website
questions.explanation: Traditional tools are reliable backups in situations where digital devices are unavailable or impractical.

questions.question: What was the main advantage of a tape recorder during an interview?
options: It replaced the need to obtain consent in all situations
It provided background knowledge on every subject
It automatically wrote the final article
It captured the conversation for accurate quotation and later transcription
questions.explanation: Recorded audio reduces dependence on memory and handwritten notes when checking direct quotations.

questions.question: Which word-processor feature most directly supports team editing at the same time?
options: A printed index
A mechanical ink ribbon
Real-time cloud collaboration
A landline dial
questions.explanation: Cloud tools such as Google Docs allow several authorised users to edit and comment on the same document simultaneously.

questions.question: What is the function of transcription software in media work?
options: Converting recorded speech into written text
Selecting newspaper page size
Replacing every source with artificial quotes
Turning text into studio lighting
questions.explanation: Transcription software speeds up the conversion of interviews and recorded events into editable text.

questions.question: Which digital resource is most suitable for quickly locating academic papers and archived information?
options: A typewriter ribbon
A studio spotlight
A paper-only telephone directory
Online research databases and search tools
questions.explanation: Search engines, Google Scholar, JSTOR, and digital archives make research and fact-checking faster.

questions.question: What is the best general principle for choosing between traditional and digital writing tools?
options: Digital tools should always replace every traditional tool
Traditional tools are always faster than digital tools
Use whichever tool is most fashionable, regardless of conditions
Use the tool that best fits the task and keep suitable backups
questions.explanation: Digital tools offer speed and flexibility, while traditional tools can be more dependable during technical failure; effective writers use both appropriately.

questions.question: Which arrangement correctly describes the inverted pyramid?
options: Most important facts first, followed by supporting and less important details
Facts placed randomly to create suspense
Background first, opinion second, facts last
Minor details first and the main fact in the conclusion
questions.explanation: The inverted pyramid prioritises essential information at the beginning and places supporting or minor details later.

questions.question: Why can an editor safely shorten an inverted-pyramid news story from the bottom?
options: The headline contains every quotation
The least essential details are usually placed near the end
The bottom always contains false information
The writer repeats the lead in every paragraph
questions.explanation: Because information descends in importance, cutting the last paragraphs should preserve the story's core facts.

questions.question: Which topic is most likely to be treated as hard news?
options: A reflective essay about childhood
A guide to decorating a bedroom
A newly announced government policy
A celebrity's favourite holiday memories
questions.explanation: Hard news covers timely and consequential events such as policy announcements, disasters, elections, and accidents.

questions.question: Which topic is most likely to be treated as soft news?
options: A sudden change in the national budget
A feature on a growing lifestyle trend
An urgent evacuation order
A breaking court judgment
questions.explanation: Soft news generally emphasises human interest, lifestyle, entertainment, analysis, or interpretation rather than urgent events.

questions.question: Which characteristic best describes an effective newspaper headline?
options: Long, vague, and filled with unexplained abbreviations
Brief, clear, active, and informative
Composed as a complete background essay
Written mainly to hide the subject of the story
questions.explanation: A headline should attract attention while communicating the story's central point quickly.

questions.question: Why do magazine features often use photographs, illustrations, and infographics?
options: To replace interviews and research
To enhance the narrative and sustain reader engagement
To eliminate the need for accurate writing
To make every article shorter than a news brief
questions.explanation: Visuals can clarify information, create mood, and deepen a longer magazine story.

questions.question: What information does a script's scene heading or slug line normally provide?
options: The complete biography of every actor
Whether the scene is interior or exterior, its location, and the time
Only the emotional state of the audience
The final production budget
questions.explanation: A slug line such as 'INT. LIVING ROOM – NIGHT' tells the team where and when the scene occurs.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an action line in a script?
options: To describe what happens visibly or physically in the scene
To provide the audience rating
To list the station's advertisers
To show the actor's salary
questions.explanation: Action lines describe movements, events, and visible behaviour that the production team must stage or record.

questions.question: Why are character names placed before dialogue in a script?
options: To indicate the location of the scene
To identify who is speaking
To show the duration of the programme
To replace all stage directions
questions.explanation: The name clearly assigns each line to the correct performer.

questions.question: What does a parenthetical such as '(angrily)' tell the performer?
options: How the following line should be delivered
How the article should be indexed online
Which camera model to purchase
Where the programme will be transmitted
questions.explanation: Parentheticals give brief performance or delivery instructions connected to dialogue.

questions.question: Why are television scripts often divided clearly around acts or commercial breaks?
options: Television scripts contain no action
Radio laws require television dialogue to stop
Film scripts cannot include scenes
Episodic television requires structured timing and break points
questions.explanation: Television production frequently works within fixed episode lengths and commercial slots, so structure and timing are explicit.

questions.question: Which element is especially important in a radio script because the audience cannot see the action?
options: Costume sketches only
Camera lens specifications
Sound-effect and music cues
Scene colours
questions.explanation: Radio relies on sound, so cues for effects, music, ambience, and vocal delivery help create the scene.

questions.question: What is a likely result of poorly formatted production scripts?
options: Automatic improvement in actors' performances
Lower need for coordination
Perfect timing without rehearsal
Confusion, mistakes, and delays among the production team
questions.explanation: Formatting is a shared production language; unclear layout can cause people to misunderstand scenes, cues, dialogue, and technical requirements.

questions.question: What makes website content scannable?
options: Hiding the main point at the end of every page
Headings, short paragraphs, lists, and clear sections
Frequent unexplained jargon
One continuous block of text
questions.explanation: Scannable structure helps screen readers locate relevant information quickly.

questions.question: What is the best use of a hyperlink in an online article?
options: Providing relevant additional context without disrupting the main message
Replacing all explanation in the article
Hiding the source of factual claims
Sending readers to unrelated pages
questions.explanation: A useful hyperlink supports the story with evidence or further detail while preserving the article's flow.

questions.question: Which tone is most commonly suitable for a personal blog?
options: Conversational and relatable
Deliberately confusing and impersonal
Written only in legal terminology
Entirely bureaucratic and distant
questions.explanation: Blogs commonly build connection through an informal, approachable voice.

questions.question: Why are regular updates useful for a blog?
options: They prevent any reader interaction
They encourage readers to return and help build a community
They make accuracy unnecessary
They remove the need for a clear topic
questions.explanation: Fresh, consistent posts maintain audience interest and create an ongoing relationship with readers.

questions.question: What responsibility accompanies the use of comment sections on a blog?
options: Treating comments as verified news reports
Deleting every opinion that differs from the writer's
Moderating discussion so it remains respectful and relevant
Allowing harassment to increase traffic
questions.explanation: Interaction can strengthen engagement, but moderation protects the quality and safety of discussion.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of hashtags in social media writing?
options: Replacing the need for a message
Preventing users from finding related content
Categorising posts and improving discoverability
Increasing the grammatical complexity of a post
questions.explanation: Relevant hashtags connect posts with topics and help interested users discover them.

questions.question: A news organisation combines a short article, an infographic, and a video interview on one page. What principle is it applying?
options: Print-only production
Tense inconsistency
Multimedia integration
Passive sourcing
questions.explanation: Digital platforms can combine complementary media forms to explain a story more dynamically.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the lead in a hard-news article?
options: To provide only the least important details
To present the reporter's personal conclusion
To list every source before stating the event
To summarise the most important facts at the beginning
questions.explanation: The lead gives readers the core of the story immediately, often answering the most important of the 5Ws and H.

questions.question: Which set correctly represents the 5Ws and H?
options: Who, which, whether, writing, why, and headline
Who, what, where, when, why, and how
What, width, web, wording, witness, and history
Where, whom, whose, will, was, and has
questions.explanation: These six questions help journalists identify and communicate the essential facts of an event.

questions.question: Which type of lead is most appropriate for a breaking report about a major earthquake?
options: A fictional dialogue lead
A review lead
A summary lead
A personal-essay lead
questions.explanation: Hard news normally needs a concise summary lead that communicates the central facts quickly.

questions.question: Which type of lead may begin by creating a mood or describing a scene?
options: A database lead
A legal notice lead
A correction lead
A feature lead
questions.explanation: Feature leads can use description, atmosphere, or narrative to draw readers into softer or more in-depth stories.

questions.question: What is normally included in the body of a news article?
options: The writer's unsupported personal beliefs
Only the headline repeated several times
Technical instructions for printing the newspaper
Supporting facts, quotations, attribution, data, and background
questions.explanation: The body expands the lead with evidence, context, source material, and increasingly less important details.

questions.question: Why is attribution important in news writing?
options: It tells readers where information or opinion came from
It removes the need to verify claims
It allows journalists to invent quotations
It guarantees that a source is correct
questions.explanation: Attribution identifies the source, supports transparency, and separates the journalist's voice from another person's claim.

questions.question: Which practice best supports objectivity in a disputed public issue?
options: Presenting relevant evidence and fairly representing multiple credible perspectives
Describing one side's opinion as unquestionable fact
Selecting only statements that support the reporter's preference
Using anonymous rumours as the main evidence
questions.explanation: Balanced reporting and clear attribution help audiences evaluate an issue without the reporter imposing a personal conclusion.

questions.question: Which sentence is clearest for a general news audience?
options: The council approved the road project on Monday.
The municipal deliberative entity effectuated authorisation of the infrastructural undertaking.
On Monday, in relation to the road project, approval was something the council did.
There was, by the council, an approval that occurred regarding a project involving a road.
questions.explanation: The sentence uses familiar words, active voice, and a direct subject-verb-object structure.

questions.question: Why do conventional news articles often lack a traditional argumentative conclusion?
options: Every article must end with the reporter's opinion
The headline legally serves as the conclusion
Their purpose is to present information, with minor details commonly placed last
Journalists are not allowed to finish sentences
questions.explanation: News stories usually end with lesser details, a quotation, or a forward-looking statement rather than an essay-style argument.

questions.question: An editor removes the final two paragraphs of an inverted-pyramid report to fit the page. Why should the report still make sense?
options: The headline contains the entire body
The essential information should already appear earlier
The final paragraphs are required to repeat the lead exactly
News articles place their main facts only in captions
questions.explanation: The inverted pyramid orders facts by importance, so the core story survives trimming from the bottom.

questions.question: What most clearly distinguishes a feature article from a hard-news report?
options: A feature cannot include interviews
A feature must always be shorter than a news brief
A feature usually explores a subject in greater depth through narrative, analysis, or human interest
A feature may never contain facts
questions.explanation: Features offer more flexible structure, description, personality, and depth while still requiring accurate reporting.

questions.question: A writer wants to explore the life, personality, and achievements of a community leader. Which feature type fits best?
options: A how-to feature
A product review
A statistical bulletin
A profile feature
questions.explanation: Profile features use interviews, observation, and background research to reveal the character and significance of a person or group.

questions.question: Which feature type is designed around ordered practical instructions?
options: A human-interest feature
A profile feature
A how-to feature
A trend feature
questions.explanation: How-to features guide readers through a task using clear steps, examples, and often visual aids.

questions.question: A story centres on a family's recovery after a disaster and aims to create emotional connection. What type is it?
options: A human-interest feature
A technical manual
A hard-news brief only
A dictionary entry
questions.explanation: Human-interest features focus on personal challenges, achievements, or touching experiences that resonate emotionally.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a personal essay?
options: It is an anonymous statistical report
It uses the writer's own experience and reflection, often in the first person
It gives only step-by-step instructions
It must exclude all personal feelings
questions.explanation: Personal essays are introspective features built around the writer's observations, experiences, and lessons.

questions.question: Which feature type normally requires extensive documents, interviews, evidence, and fact-checking to reveal hidden wrongdoing?
options: A routine weather brief
A personal diary entry
An investigative feature
A travel feature
questions.explanation: Investigative features uncover significant information through sustained research, verification, and evidence.

questions.question: A writer examines why a new social-media behaviour is spreading and what effects it may have. Which feature type is most suitable?
options: A how-to feature
A breaking-news alert
A trend feature
A profile feature
questions.explanation: Trend features analyse emerging or continuing patterns, their causes, implications, data, and expert views.

questions.question: What should a balanced review feature contain?
options: An evidence-based assessment of both strengths and weaknesses
Only praise supplied by the manufacturer
Unverified attacks on the creator
A plot summary with no evaluation
questions.explanation: A useful review evaluates the subject fairly and supports recommendations with reasons and experience.

questions.question: How does observation strengthen feature research?
options: It allows the writer to invent scenes
It guarantees access to private information
It captures atmosphere, behaviour, sensory detail, and real-life interaction
It replaces the need to verify factual claims
questions.explanation: Careful observation provides vivid details that interviews and documents may not reveal.

questions.question: During an interview, a source mentions an unexpected but important experience. What should the feature writer do?
options: Ignore it because it was not in the prepared list
End the interview immediately
Listen actively and ask a relevant follow-up question
Change the quotation to fit the original plan
questions.explanation: Prepared questions provide direction, but active listening allows the writer to explore valuable unplanned material.

questions.question: Which sentence best demonstrates 'show, don't tell' in character development?
options: Amina was emotional.
The writer says that Amina was very sad.
Amina gripped the letter, took a slow breath, and wiped her eyes.
Amina had feelings about the letter.
questions.explanation: Actions and sensory details reveal emotion more vividly than simply naming it.

questions.question: What ethical principle requires an opinion writer to use correct and verifiable evidence?
options: Popularity
Sensationalism
Anonymity
Accuracy
questions.explanation: Opinion pieces may be subjective, but any factual claims used to support them must still be accurate and verifiable.

questions.question: What does fairness require when an opinion article addresses a contentious issue?
options: Allowing rumours to replace documented facts
Representing relevant opposing viewpoints honestly
Ignoring every argument that challenges the writer
Pretending all evidence has equal quality
questions.explanation: Fairness means engaging opposing perspectives accurately and respectfully rather than misrepresenting or concealing them.

questions.question: How can an opinion writer demonstrate transparency?
options: Avoid identifying the basis of an argument
Clearly distinguish personal judgement from factual claims
Present every personal belief as established fact
Hide the evidence used in the article
questions.explanation: Phrases and sourcing can make clear what is the writer's view and what is supported by evidence.

questions.question: What does accountability require after an opinion writer discovers a factual error?
options: Correct the error promptly and openly
Delete all evidence without explanation
Blame readers for misunderstanding it
Leave it unchanged to protect the writer's image
questions.explanation: Accountability means accepting responsibility for claims and correcting mistakes when they are identified.

questions.question: What is cherry-picking in opinion writing?
options: Checking a claim through several independent sources
Quoting an opposing view accurately
Separating facts from opinions
Selecting only evidence that supports a position while ignoring relevant contrary evidence
questions.explanation: Cherry-picking creates a misleading picture by presenting a selective sample of the available evidence.

questions.question: What is false equivalency?
options: Using several verified statistics
Correcting a misleading comparison
Explaining why one source is more reliable
Presenting two unequal positions as though the evidence supporting them were equal
questions.explanation: False equivalency can mislead readers by giving unsupported or weak claims the same weight as well-established evidence.

questions.question: Which consequence can follow from publishing an unsupported allegation that damages a person's reputation?
options: Guaranteed growth in public trust
Automatic protection because it appeared in an opinion column
Removal of all ethical responsibility
Loss of credibility and possible defamation proceedings
questions.explanation: Opinion labels do not excuse false harmful factual claims; the writer may lose trust and face legal consequences.

questions.question: What makes interactive storytelling different from a purely linear article?
options: It contains no text
It can only be distributed in print
The audience can participate, explore options, or control parts of the experience
It prevents users from accessing additional information
questions.explanation: Interactive stories let users click, choose, respond, or explore material rather than follow only one fixed path.

questions.question: In a multimedia story, what should text do when an image already communicates the basic visual information?
options: Add context, explanation, or details that complement the image
Ignore the main subject
Become longer than every other element combined
Repeat the image's obvious content word for word
questions.explanation: Multimedia elements should work together; text should deepen understanding rather than duplicate what is already visible.

questions.question: Which visual format is best suited to simplifying a complex set of statistics?
options: A long block of dialogue
An infographic
An uncaptioned decorative photograph
A scene heading
questions.explanation: Infographics organise data visually, helping audiences identify patterns and understand complex information quickly.

questions.question: Why should online videos usually include captions or subtitles?
options: To replace the need for accurate audio
To increase the length of every clip
To make the video impossible to understand without sound
To improve accessibility and support viewing in different environments
questions.explanation: Captions support people with hearing difficulties and viewers watching without sound, while also reinforcing comprehension.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a storyboard in multimedia production?
options: Choosing the legal owner of the platform
Calculating the journalist's salary
Replacing all research and scripting
Planning how text, images, video, and interactive elements will be sequenced
questions.explanation: A storyboard helps creators visualise the structure, placement, and relationship of different media elements before production.

questions.question: Which SEO practice is most appropriate for a web article?
options: Using relevant keywords naturally and writing an informative meta description
Avoiding descriptive headlines and summaries
Repeating one keyword in every sentence
Hiding unrelated keywords in the article
questions.explanation: Effective SEO improves discoverability without damaging readability; relevant keywords and clear meta descriptions help search engines and users understand the page.
